The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

Both findings are fixed inside the figure briefs; no application text changed.

The disclosure says handles exist and what they are for but not where one attaches, so the drawing convention is now explicitly labelled as such. Nothing corresponding was added to the Brief Description of the Drawings or the detailed description, which stay position-neutral.

Two consequential adjustments were needed to keep the briefs legal after those additions. FIG. 1 rose to 2820 characters and FIG. 5 to 2847, both over the 2800 limit, so I recovered length from wording rather than content: shorter endpoint phrasing on FIG. 1 (each target still names the same part and the same broad region), and on FIG. 5 the removal of the cord's line-weight and single-stroke rendering instruction, which was a generic linework control. The cord is still specified as one slack curved path drawn as a single continuous curved line, which is what the drawing rules call for. The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left. Outline line work only, with no lettering drawn.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile in perspective, filling the lower part of the drawing area. The machine stands on its left-hand part, leaving a wide open expanse of tile to the right.

The machine is one plain rectangular slab, the base 12, standing on a band that runs round its underside. Three closed blocks stand side by side on the top face of the slab, clear of one another: the left-hand block is the vibration motor 18, the middle block is the grip, and the right-hand block is the air-extraction mechanism 20. Each has a broad front face turned toward the viewer, large enough for a point well inside it to stand clear of its edges. Slab, band, blocks and tile are shown schematically, these rectangular forms being a convention for this sheet only, and the position of the grip on the slab and relative to the other two blocks is a placement convention for this sheet only that asserts no particular mounting location.

The slab is drawn thick, its front face turned toward the viewer as the largest plain surface of the machine, running the whole width below the blocks and above the band, deep enough for a point well inside it to stand clear of its upper and lower edges.

The band meets the underside of the slab and follows the same rectangular run, its front surface facing the viewer as one unbroken strip running the whole width between that underside and the tile, deep enough for a point well inside it to stand clear of the underside above and the tile below; its depth is schematic and no proportion is asserted. The band stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting the tile.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine. Identified on the outer boundary of the machine, the silhouette line at which slab, band and blocks together stand against the open background, at any place along it.
- The base 12 is the slab. Identified well inside its front face, the large upright surface below the three blocks and above the band.
- The vibration motor 18 is the left-hand block. Identified well inside its front face.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is the right-hand block. Identified well inside its front face.
- The perimeter member 24 is the band beneath the slab. Identified well inside its front strip, between the underside of the slab and the tile.
- The covering element 36 is the tile. Identified well inside the open expanse of tile to its right.
- The handle 44 is the middle block. Identified well inside its front face.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44

# FIG. 5 - Second embodiment with a pulling element

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1. Outline line work only, with no lettering drawn. The vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism are omitted.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile seen in perspective, as in FIG. 1, filling the lower part of the drawing area. The machine stands on its right-hand part, leaving a wide open expanse of tile to the left.

The machine and the tile are shown schematically, the machine as one plain rectangular body standing on a band that runs round its underside, the band alone touching the tile, these forms being a depiction convention for this sheet only. The body and the band are the whole of the machine drawn on this sheet.

The band meets the underside of the body and follows the same rectangular run, its front surface facing the viewer as a broad strip between that underside and the tile; the depth of the strip is shown schematically and no particular proportion is asserted. The band stands on the tile with its lower edge meeting the tile, and an open stretch of tile lies in front of the machine.

The flexible pulling element 46 is drawn as one slack curved path, in the manner of a loose cord: a single continuous curved line. It begins where it meets the left-hand side of the machine, that meeting place being shown schematically with no attachment formation shown, and runs away to the left, sagging gently over the open expanse of tile; its free end is the point at which that single line stops, well inside the left-hand limit of the drawing area.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine standing on the covering element 36, the rectangular body with its band. Identified on the outer boundary of the machine, the silhouette line at which the rectangular body and its band together stand against the open background, at any place along that line clear of the flexible pulling element 46.
- The perimeter member 24 is the band under the rectangular body. Identified well inside the broad front strip of the band, below the underside of the rectangular body and above the tile, clear of both of those boundaries.
- The flexible pulling element 46 is that slack curved path. Identified on the path where it runs over the open expanse of tile, clear of the machine.
- The covering element 36 is that large plain tile, on which the machine stands. Identified well inside that open stretch of tile in front of the machine, clear of the machine and of the flexible pulling element 46.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 24, 36, 46

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet shows the perimeter member 24 as one rectangular ring, and within it the second side 16 as a plain open field; no other body is drawn. The ring is the perimeter member 24 seen end on, shown schematically with a rectangular plan outline, this being a depiction convention for this sheet only.

The ring is drawn as one rectangle with a smaller rectangle inside it, the inner rectangle standing well in from each of the four sides of the outer rectangle. The band of paper lying between the outer rectangle and the inner rectangle is the drawn body. It runs continuously all the way round, turning each of the four corners without interruption, and it is broad along each of its four sides, its outer edge and its inner edge standing far enough apart for the band to read plainly as a surface of its own; the width of that band is shown schematically and no particular proportion is asserted.

The band carries round each corner as one continuous surface, so that the ring reads as one closed body running between its outer edge and its inner edge.

The field enclosed by the inner rectangle is left entirely open paper.

The ring stands well in from every side of the drawing area, so that the outer rectangle reads plainly as the edge of the ring.

- The perimeter member 24 is the band of the ring, the surface lying between its outer edge and its inner edge. - The second side 16 is the underside face that this view looks straight at, and it shows within the perimeter member 24 as the plain field inside the inner edge of the ring. Identified well inside that field, away from the band.

All three sheets are repaired at the geometry level, where the endpoint failures actually originate.

**FIG. 1 (numerals 12 and 44 misplaced).** The two rejected targets were the thin front face of the slab and a small grip block competing with two similar housings. The sheet now draws three closed blocks standing side by side on the top face, named by stable position: the left-hand block is the vibration motor 18, the middle block is the grip, the right-hand block is the air-extraction mechanism 20, each with a broad front face drawn large enough for an interior point to clear its edges. The base 12 is now the large surface below all three blocks and above the band, and the slab is specified thick enough for a point well inside that face to clear its upper and lower edges. The handle 44 target is the middle block's front face, which is a stable positional reference rather than a shape the annotator has to find. The placement disclaimer added last turn is retained, so the grip's position still asserts no mounting location.

**FIG. 5 (numeral 24 misplaced).** The band's front surface is now specified as one unbroken strip running the whole width of the machine, deep enough for a point well inside it to clear the underside above and the tile below, and the numeral target is that interior surface. The same wording now governs the band on FIG. 1, so the perimeter member is labelled the same way on both perspective sheets.

**FIG. 3 (independent endpoint audit).** Both targets on this sheet sit inside a rectangular ring, so each region is now required to be wide enough to hold an interior point clear of its bounding edges: the band between the outer and inner rectangles, and the field within the inner rectangle. The perimeter member 24 target is anchored to the left-hand side of the ring, and the second side 16 target is the enclosed field clear of the band all round.

All five briefs are under the 2800-character limit (2795, 2591, 2161, 2768, 2793), each declaration still matches its sheet list, all 16 numerals remain covered across the sheets, and no claim, description, drawing description, or numeral definition was touched.

input.summary: Repaired the three failing sheets by enlarging the target regions and naming each target by a stable position rather than by shape. FIG. 1 now shows three side-by-side blocks on the top face (left is the vibration motor 18, middle is the grip, right is the air-extraction mechanism 20) over a thick slab whose front face is the largest surface on the machine, fixing the rejected endpoints for base 12 and handle 44. FIG. 5's band is specified as one unbroken full-width strip deep enough to hold an interior point, fixing numeral 24. FIG. 3 requires both the ring band and the enclosed field to be wide enough for an interior point clear of their edges, with 24 anchored to the left-hand side of the ring. No application text changed.
reasoning: All three failures were rejected coordinate clusters, which is a geometry problem rather than a wording problem. Restating the same target in new words would have produced the same thin region, so in each case I enlarged the region the renderer must draw and then pointed the numeral at it.

On FIG. 1 the base 12 target failed because the slab's front face is a narrow horizontal strip when the housings above it dominate the machine. The slab is now specified thick, with its front face the largest plain surface on the machine, running the whole width below the blocks and above the band, so the interior point has room.

The handle 44 target failed because a grip sitting between two similar housings is hard to single out. Naming the three bodies as left-hand, middle and right-hand blocks turns every top-face target into a positional reference, which is the disambiguation the drawing rules call for, and it removes any need for the annotator to identify a part by its shape.

I kept the placement disclaimer for the grip that the previous review required. Calling the grip the middle block is a page position, and the brief still says the position on the slab and relative to the other two blocks asserts no mounting location, so the positional naming does not smuggle back an untraced mounting relationship.

FIG. 5's numeral 24 and FIG. 1's numeral 24 label the same kind of thin skirt strip, so I gave both sheets the same specification: one unbroken strip running the whole width, deep enough for a point well inside it to clear the underside above and the tile below. Fixing only the sheet that failed would have left the other one waiting to fail.

FIG. 3's audit gave no numeral, and the sheet has only two targets, both inside a rectangular ring, so I treated both as suspect: the band and the enclosed field must each be wide enough to hold an interior point clear of their bounding edges. Anchoring 24 to the left-hand side of the ring replaces the vague 'at any place along it' with a named side while keeping a broad region.

Every enlargement is stated as schematic with no proportion asserted, because the disclosure gives no dimensions for the base, the perimeter member, or the tile. The depth requirements are depiction conventions for the sheets, not asserted structure.

The additions pushed FIG. 1 to 3117 characters and FIG. 5 over the limit, so I compressed wording rather than dropping content: redundant restatements of the blocks and the band went, and every part, contact, and target region survived. FIG. 1 is 2795 and FIG. 5 is 2793.

# FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left. Outline line work only, with no lettering drawn.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile in perspective filling the lower drawing area. The machine stands on its left-hand part, leaving a wide open expanse of tile to the right.

The machine is one plain rectangular slab, the base 12, standing on a band that runs round its underside. Three closed blocks stand side by side on its top face, clear of one another: the left-hand block is the vibration motor 18, the middle block is the handle 44, and the right-hand block is the air-extraction mechanism 20. Slab, band, blocks and tile are shown schematically, these rectangular forms being a convention for this sheet only; the position of the handle 44 on the slab and relative to the other blocks is a placement convention asserting no mounting location.

The slab is drawn thick, its front face turned toward the viewer as the largest surface of the machine, running the whole width below the blocks and above the band, and drawn tall and broad enough to hold a point well away from all four of its edges.

Each block is drawn broad and tall, its front face turned toward the viewer as a large plain surface, likewise able to hold a point well away from all four of its edges.

The band meets the underside of the slab and follows the same rectangular run, its front surface facing the viewer as one unbroken strip across the whole width between that underside and the tile, deep enough for a point well inside it to clear both; its depth is schematic and no proportion is asserted. It stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting the tile.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area, the machine drawn large within it and turned so that the front faces of the slab and of the three blocks are the broad surfaces presented to the viewer.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine. Identified on the outer boundary of the machine, where its silhouette stands against the open background.
- The base 12 is the slab. Identified in the interior of its front face, well away from every edge of that face.
- The vibration motor 18 is the left-hand block. Identified well inside its front face.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is the right-hand block. Identified well inside its front face.
- The perimeter member 24 is the band beneath the slab. Identified well inside its front strip, between the slab underside and the tile.
- The covering element 36 is the tile. Identified well inside the open expanse of tile to its right.
- The handle 44 is the middle block. Identified in the interior of its front face, well away from every edge of that face.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left. Outline line work only, with no lettering drawn.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile in perspective filling the lower drawing area. The machine stands on its left-hand part, leaving a wide open expanse of tile to the right.

The machine is one plain rectangular slab, the base 12, standing on a band that runs round its underside. Three closed blocks stand side by side on its top face, clear of one another: the left-hand block is the vibration motor 18, the middle block is the handle 44, and the right-hand block is the air-extraction mechanism 20. Slab, band, blocks and tile are shown schematically, these rectangular forms being a convention for this sheet only; the position of the handle 44 on the slab and relative to the other blocks is a placement convention asserting no mounting location.

The slab is drawn thick, its front face turned toward the viewer as the largest surface of the machine, running the whole width below the blocks and above the band, and drawn tall and broad enough to hold a point well away from all four of its edges.

Each block is drawn broad and tall, its front face turned toward the viewer as a large plain surface, likewise able to hold a point well away from all four of its edges.

The band meets the underside of the slab and follows the same rectangular run, its front surface facing the viewer as one unbroken strip across the whole width between that underside and the tile, deep enough for a point well inside it to clear both; its depth is schematic and no proportion is asserted. It stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting the tile.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area, the machine drawn large within it and turned so that the front faces of the slab and of the three blocks are the broad surfaces presented to the viewer.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine. Identified on the outer boundary of the machine, where its silhouette stands against the open background.
- The base 12 is the slab. Identified in the interior of its front face, well away from every edge of that face.
- The vibration motor 18 is the left-hand block. Identified well inside its front face.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is the right-hand block. Identified well inside its front face.
- The perimeter member 24 is the band beneath the slab. Identified well inside its front strip, between the slab underside and the tile.
- The covering element 36 is the tile. Identified well inside the open expanse of tile to its right.
- The handle 44 is the middle block. Identified in the interior of its front face, well away from every edge of that face.

content.text:
The one failing sheet is repaired.

**FIG. 1, numerals 12 and 44.** Both dots landed on a boundary line rather than inside a face: numeral 12 near the corner where the slab's front and left faces meet, numeral 44 on the top edge of the middle block's front face. The repair works on both halves of the problem.

Geometry: the machine is now drawn large within the drawing area and turned so that the front faces of the slab and the blocks are the broad surfaces presented to the viewer. The slab's front face must be tall and broad enough to hold a point well away from all four of its edges, and each block's front face likewise. That gives the annotator room it did not have when those faces rendered as narrow strips.

Targets: numeral 12 is now identified in the interior of the slab's front face, well away from every edge of that face, and numeral 44 in the interior of the middle block's front face on the same terms. Both remain broad interior regions with no midpoint, depth, or quarter modifier, and each part is still named by stable position, so the middle block continues to identify the handle 44.

Length stayed within the limit by compressing lower-risk wording: the band and silhouette sentences say the same thing in fewer words, and the perimeter member 24 target keeps its front-strip region. FIG. 1 is 2799 characters, the other four briefs are unchanged, every declaration matches its sheet list, all 16 numerals remain covered, and no claim, description, drawing description, or numeral definition was touched.

input.summary: Repaired the FIG. 1 endpoint failures for numerals 12 and 44. The slab's front face and each block's front face must now be drawn large enough to hold a point well away from all four edges, the machine is drawn large and turned so those front faces are the broad surfaces presented to the viewer, and both numerals now target the interior of their face well away from every edge. Compressed other wording to keep the brief at 2799 characters. No application text, claim, or numeral definition changed.
reasoning: The report gave raw coordinates showing both dots on boundary lines: numeral 12 by the corner where the slab's front and left faces meet, numeral 44 on the top edge of the middle block's front face. That is a room problem, so the repair had to enlarge the faces as well as reword the targets; repeating 'well inside its front face' would have produced the same cramped region.
